item.title: When you hit ‘delete’, what really happens to your data?
item.description: There is a pressing need for provision of concise, accessible and clear information about how deletion really works.
item.content:encoded:
Deletion is a common part of modern life. We send files and folders to the recycle bin all the time, and often get rid of unwanted personal accounts. But do you know what really happens when you hit the “delete” button?

The process of deletion is often poorly explained by tech providers. Lack of transparency around how requests are processed, and the absence of clear confirmation that data has been removed, are frequently highlighted in research.

These issues are not limited to operating systems. On social media platforms and a wide range of subscription services, deletion mechanisms are often just as unclear. Such misconceptions can have serious implications for the wellbeing of users, exposing them to security and privacy vulnerabilities.

A further complication is that many users fear losing data, files, photos and videos through accidental deletion – a condition dubbed “diagraphephobia”. Though this is not a recognised pathology, studies of digital hoarding behaviour show that some people get very anxious at the thought of losing or accidentally deleting personal information such as photos and music.

Such concerns extend the amount of personal data that sits untended but undeleted, ready for potential misappropriation.

item.title: Bareilly’s Islamic religious event drops meat from menu, changes dates because of Kanwar Yatra
item.description: The organisers said the decisions were taken after the district administration and police raised concerns about the movement of kanwariyas.
item.content:encoded:
Meat has been removed from the menu of an Islamic religious event in Uttar Pradesh’s Bareilly in view of the ongoing Kanwar Yatra, The Indian Express reported.

The organisers said that the decision was taken based on a request by the district administration and the police.

The event is the 108th Urs-e-Razvi, a three-day annual commemoration of the death anniversary of the 19th-century Sufi scholar Imam Ahmad Raza Khan Barelvi. Devotees from around the world are expected to attend.

The administration of Ala Hazrat Dargah – the shrine of Barelvi – has also rescheduled the event, which falls during the Hindu month of Sawan this year. It will now be held from August 6 to August 8 instead of August 7 to August 9.

During the Kanwar Yatra, devotees, called kanwariyas, walk hundreds of kilometres to collect water from the Ganga near Haridwar and carry it back to their home states to offer at temples. The Kanwar Yatra began on July 30 and will end on August 11.

Media in-charge of the Ala Hazrat Dargah Nasir Qureshi said that the decision to “change the dates was taken keeping in mind the presence of large numbers of Kanwariyas in the city, as well as a request from the district administration and police”, The Indian Express reported.

item.title: India brought back 274 fugitives from 36 countries since 2019, says Centre
item.description: Among them, 62 criminals were wanted for murder, robbery or other violent crimes, and 53 for sexual offences, including those booked under Pocso.
item.content:encoded:
The Indian government has brought back 274 fugitives from 36 countries since 2019, stated the Ministry of Home Affairs on Tuesday.

Among them, 62 criminals were wanted for murder, robbery or other violent crimes, and 53 for sexual offences, including those booked under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, the ministry added.

It stated that 17 of the fugitives were booked for terrorist or anti-national activities, and 16 for offences under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, which bans the production, possession, use and sale of illegal drugs.

Nine of the fugitives brought back were accused of financial crimes, said the home ministry.

While nine of the fugitives were brought back in 2019, only seven were repatriated in 2020. In 2021, the Indian government brought back 23 fugitives and the number increased to 40 in 2022.

Thirty-seven of the fugitives were repatriated in 2023, 43 in 2024, 70 in 2025 and 45 so far in 2026, said the ministry.

It added that in the last three years, Red Corner notices have been issued against 401 fugitives.

item.content:encoded:
Ten passengers and four crew members on board an Air India flight from Phuket to Delhi were injured after the aircraft experienced sudden loss of altitude, the Hindustan Times reported.

An unidentified official of the Directorate General of Civil Aviation said that the pilot reported “sudden loss” of approximately 300 feet of altitude, PTI reported.

One cabin crew member was severely injured, the official added.

The aviation regulator will conduct an investigation into the incident, the news agency quoted the official as saying.

The plane, an Airbus A320 aircraft, took off from Phuket at 8.25 am and landed in Delhi at 11 am.

However, the institute said that the 85-year-old convict needs round-the-clock assistance by trained caregivers.

The matter will be heard further on Thursday.

The directive had come after the religious leader’s counsel informed the court that he had developed “acute internal bleeding”.

On June 30, the Supreme Court rejected Asaram’s bail plea, saying that it would consider granting it only if there was a grave medical necessity, “such as danger to life”.

item.description: Without evidence, judicial interference in the evaluation process would undermine the sanctity of the examination system, the bench observed.
item.content:encoded:
The Chhattisgarh High Court has observed that allegations of tampering with the answer sheet of a candidate of the 2026 National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test cannot be accepted solely on the basis of suspicion, conjecture or subjective belief in the absence of evidence, The Indian Express reported on Tuesday.

A bench led by Chief Justice Ramesh Sinha dismissed the candidate’s petition, holding that judicial interference in the evaluation process based only on a person’s apprehensions would undermine the certainty, sanctity and finality of the examination system.

The court was hearing a petition filed by a candidate who appeared in the undergraduate NEET re-examination held on June 21 after the original test was cancelled following alleged paper leaks. The results of the re-examination were declared on July 16.

Subsequently, some candidates alleged that the optical mark recognition answer sheets uploaded against their roll numbers did not belong to them, had been interchanged or showed fewer attempted answers than they had marked.

Optical mark recognition is a system that reads answers marked by candidates by detecting filled bubbles or marks on an answer sheet.

item.content:encoded:
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India has prohibited five manufacturers from selling popular rum and whisky drinks for not complying with regulations, said the Ministry of Health and Welfare on Monday.

The manufacturers had been using added flavours rather than relying on the maturation of base materials such as molasses or malt to develop the products’ taste and aroma, the ministry added.

It said that based on the appeal by two manufacturers, “conditional revocation has been issued”.

“For the existing stock in hand, they have been allowed to sell the product by revealing the true nature of the product on the front of the pack, whereas for future production a clear direction has been passed as to not add identical flavour in the product, such as rum flavour or whisky flavour,” said the ministry.

It pointed out that such products are not only sub-standard, “but are also misrepresented by using the names of standard categories”. “At best, they can be identified as rum-flavoured spirit or whisky-flavoured spirit, etc,” it said.

item.title: Long considered sacred, the golden langur, found in western Assam, is now an endangered animal
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Mammals of India’, by AJT Johnsingh and PO Nameer.
item.content:encoded:
Being confined to the sal-dominated (Shorea robusta) tropical moist deciduous and semi-evergreen forests in India, and the sub-tropical and temperate broad-leaved forests in the India – Bhutan landscape, the golden langur stands out as the most restricted colobine (leaf-eating primate) species in India. Although described by earlier naturalists such as RB Pemberton and CM Inglis and co-workers during the 19th century as “cream colored monkey” and “Sankosh cream langurs”, the credit for suggesting that it could be a new species goes to EP Gee, a British tea planter and conservationist living in Assam. It was formally described in 1956 by H Khajuria of the Zoological Survey of India and named Presbytis geei in honour of Gee.

The golden langur is a medium-sized primate. Males weigh 10-12 kg and females 9.5-10 kg. They are less sexually dimorphic than other colobines such as grey langurs (Semnopithecus spp). Based on phylogeny and biogeography, T Wangchuk, a Bhutanese biologist, opined that Trachypithecus geei and T pileatus (capped langurs) branched off from an ancestral Trachypithecus from South Asia. In addition, the Sankosh River and Pele La mountain system in central Bhutan isolated a population of capped langurs during a warming period in central Bhutan, and this population later specialised into the morphologically distinct golden langur.

item.title: Change in transgender law cannot cancel rights already given, Supreme Court tells Centre
item.description: The amendments to the 2019 Act give the government complete power to determine gender identity and invalidate transgender cards, the petitioners contended.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court on Monday verbally clarified to the Union government that the 2026 amendments to the Transgender Persons Protection of Rights Act will not retrospectively or by default invalidate transgender cards issued to members of the community under the previous legislation, The Hindu reported.

The amendments to the 2019 Act, cleared by Parliament in March, redefine who qualifies as a transgender person. They remove transgender persons’ right to a self-perceived gender identity. They also limit the scope of the law to those with certain biological or physiological characteristics, intersex variations, or specific socio-cultural identities such as kinner, hijra, aravani and jogta.

The law makes medical evaluation and certification mandatory for legal gender recognition. It underlines that the authority to permit such transitions is vested in medical professionals operating under a medical board.

On Monday, petitioners against the amendments, who include members of the transgender community and activists, contended that the amendments give the government complete power to determine gender identity, The Hindu reported. Transgender cards issued by the government cannot be invalidated as they are an essential identity document, the petitioners said.

The counsel representing one of the petitioners sought an interim order for the government to maintain the status quo.

item.title: 22 children have died of Chandipura virus infection in Gujarat: Health minister
item.description: The deaths have taken place since the first week of July, with all those infected being below 15 years of age.
item.content:encoded:
Twenty-two children have died due to Chandipura Vesiculovirus infection in Gujarat since the first week of July, The Indian Express quoted the state’s Health Minister Praful Pansheriya as saying.

Seven patients who tested positive are undergoing treatment at various civil hospitals, while six others have recovered and been discharged.

In a statement issued on Monday, the health minister’s office said that Gujarat has registered 184 suspected Chandipura virus cases so far, the newspaper reported. Among them, 35 were confirmed as positive, while the test results of 11 suspected cases were pending as of August 3.

All those infected are below 15 years of age, The Hindu reported.

The virus, also known as the Chandipura Viral Encephalitis, is transmitted primarily by sandflies and mosquitoes, including the Aedes aegypti species that bite during the day and is also known to spread dengue. The infection can lead to encephalitis, or the inflammation of the active tissues of the brain.

Children under the age of 15 years are most susceptible to the virus. Symptoms include fever, vomiting, altered sensorium, convulsions, diarrhoea, neurological deficit and meningeal irritation.

Pansheriya said on Monday that children admitted to hospitals at Gandhinagar, Himmatnagar, Patan, Rajkot and Bhavnagar are being given specialised treatment, The Hindu reported.

Neither Biswapati Sarkar nor Sameer Saxena, the creators of the Prime Video series Adarsh Baal Vidyalala, studied in a government school. But Sarkar and Saxena both had family members who taught in government-run educational institutions – a connection that helped them build the riotous world explored across the show’s seven episodes, they told Scroll.

Directed by Himank Gaur, the Hindi series follows the misadventures of Adarsh Baal Vidyalala’s principal Gyaneshwar as he tries to turn around his run-down school’s reputation. Gyaneshwar hopes that by achieving better results in the tenth standard examination, he will be selected for a training programme in the United Kingdom. With everything lax in his school, starting with himself, it’s a tall order, as events prove.

The series deploys satire to explore the problems facing government-aided schools, from poor facilities and anarchic students to political interference and restless parents.

item.title: Undone by a meme: Mockery may have dealt a shock to the Modi-led regime – history shows why
item.description: Despite media control, the information environment suddenly changed, and the government had long banned one platform where it could have seen warning signs.

On a chilly morning in December 1989, Romanian President Nicolae Ceaușescu stepped onto the balcony of the Communist Party headquarters in Bucharest to deliver a speech. The crowd was full with people holding up carrying massive pictures of the version of him, and of his wife Elena.

Ceaușescu was very particular about how he looked on photographs – a team made sure wrinkles were removed and any photo looked perfectly staged. The widely circulated large posters of him had him in his 40s, people in Romania marveled at how his official posters refused to age. Like an unfortunate analogy for South Indian movie stardom, the crowd waving posters of the yesteryear blockbuster, facing an arthritic live version.

At first, the event seemed to be going alright. There were the usual celebratory chants, revolutionary slogans being waved on large red banners, the perfected dictatorship-style choreographed clapping lining the speech. Then something unexpected happened. Someone booed, then another person booed, and another. Within seconds the entire crowd burst into aggressive heckling.

item.title: Justice MS Liberhan, who headed commission to probe Babri Masjid demolition, dies
item.description: He retired as the chief justice of the Andhra Pradesh High Court on November 10, 2000, but continued to serve as the head of the Liberhan Commission.
item.content:encoded:
Justice Manmohan Singh Liberhan, who headed a one-man judicial commission to investigate the circumstances that led to the demolition of the Babri Masjid in Ayodhya, died at the age of 87 on Sunday, The Hindu reported.

His last rites were performed on Monday.

Born on November 11, 1938, in a village near Chandigarh, Liberhan was a former Chief Justice of the Andhra Pradesh and Madras High Courts.

He began his career at the Punjab and Haryana High Court in 1964.

On February 11, 1987, Liberhan was elevated as a judge of the Punjab and Haryana High Court.

He retired as the chief justice of the Andhra Pradesh High Court on November 10, 2000, but continued to serve as the head of the Liberhan Commission.

The commission was set up days after the Babri Masjid was demolished on December 6, 1992 by Hindutva extremists who believed that the site was the birthplace of the deity Ram. It submitted its report to the Union government after 17 years, in 2009.

It went on to become one of the longest-running commissions of inquiry in India’s history.

The panel indicted Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh members for their alleged involvement in destroying the mosque. It also named several senior leaders of the Bharatiya Janata Party such as Atal Bihari Vajpayee, LK Advani, Kalyan Singh, Pramod Mahajan and others.

Shweta Patil, a teacher in Mumbai, is currently working two jobs.

As class teacher, the 37-year-old handles 39 second-standard students in Sion’s DS High School, a private school that is partly funded by the government, from morning till late afternoon. In her second shift, she works as a booth level officer carrying out the special intensive revision of electoral rolls.

The Maharashtra Election Commission allocated 1,159 voters in Mahim assembly constituency to Patil. She had to map the voters first, then fill their enumeration forms. The deadline for submitting the forms is August 8. But until July end, she had managed to fill forms of only 200-odd voters.

“It is not just me,” she said. “Every BLO is struggling. I have been a teacher for 15 years but I have never been so frustrated in my life.”

Patil pointed to her incessantly ringing mobile phone. “The Election Commission gave my personal number to voters without my permission,” she said. “I get over 50 calls a day. Callers yell at me because their name is not on the 2002 SIR list or because they did not get an enumeration form.”

item.title: Bali’s fishing canoes are vanishing as tourism changes Indonesia’s coastline
item.description: The traditional boats with colourful carvings of the mythical elephant-fish on their prows represent centuries of maritime heritage.
item.content:encoded:
Five decades ago, Bali’s coastline was adorned with traditional fishing canoes with colourful carvings of mythical elephant-fish. Where did they go?

The disappearance of these canoes tells a much bigger story about how tourism, collecting and coastal change are reshaping Indonesia’s living maritime heritage – and why preserving these traditions matters.

The boats that once lined Bali’s beaches

Before Bali became one of the worlds’ most popular tourist destinations, fishing villages lined the beaches of Benoa, Nusa Dua and Sanur, along the island’s southern coast.

Generations of fishers built and sailed jukung pelasan – traditional timber double-outrigger sailing canoes with colourful carved gajah mina (elephant-fish) prows.

The gajah mina is a creature in Balinese Hindu tradition with the head of an elephant and the body of a fish. Symbolising unity and harmony between land and sea, it is said to protect crews during voyages and provide safe passage.

These were not just fishing boats; they were central to daily life in southern Bali.

The jukung were symbols of status and community identity. They embodied generations of craftsmanship, spiritual belief and maritime knowledge. They expressed the economic, social and spiritual life of Bali’s coastal communities, and reflected the enduring relationship between its people and the sea.

Today, however, only a handful remain.

item.title: Karnataka Congress MLA resigns after DK Shivakumar announces first Cabinet expansion

Patil said that he had been “hurt” for being overlooked for a ministerial berth.

“I have been in politics for four decades,” the newspaper quoted Patil as saying. He added that he would decide whether he would quit the party or not.

Another Congress MLA Belur Gopalkrishna also said that he would resign from the Assembly as well as the chairperson of the Karnataka State Forest Industries Corporation.

“Only if you are children of chief ministers or ministers, will you have a chance [of becoming a minister]...,” The Indian Express quoted Gopalkrishna as saying.

Of the 20 MLAs inducted on Monday, 10 are first-time ministers, The Hindu reported.

“There are many MLAs,” The Indian Express quoted Shivakumar as saying. “...Earlier, I too missed out on a ministerial berth in the Siddaramaiah Cabinet. But didn’t I become a minister later?”

Shivakumar became the chief minister of Karnataka on June 3, replacing Siddaramaiah.

item.title: India’s rhetoric on a two-state solution in Palestine is at odds with Israel’s geographic reordering
item.description: This language describes a country that no longer exists in any contiguous form while Israel expands its grip on the region.
item.content:encoded:
On July 7, Narendra Modi stood beside Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto in Jakarta and declared that India supports “a two-state solution and the pursuit of lasting peace” in Palestine. Modi was repeating a line that Indian prime ministers have recited for decades. It is a comfortable formulation that costs New Delhi nothing and offends no one.

A week later, Indian officials at the Palestine Donor Group meetings in Brussels reiterated the commitment, welcoming diplomatic avenues towards Palestinian statehood and UN membership.

But this language now describes a country that no longer exists in any coherent, contiguous form, and every week that passes widens the gap between rhetoric and reality.

On July 14, just a week after Modi’s Jakarta remarks, Israel’s security cabinet approved a budget of $434 million to establish 34 new settlements in the occupied West Bank. This is the latest move in a wider settlement project, the scale of which makes the two-state framework difficult to sustain in its classical sense.

Israel’s settler expansion has drawn criticism abroad, but the same chasm between word and deed is visible closer to home. India has kept up its rhetorical support for Palestinian statehood even as it deepens its own ties with Israel.

We are bunkered down in the house, no contact with the world outside. My husband watches television all day. The news laps against my ears like waves at high tide. I constantly find myself in the kitchen – cooking, cleaning, doing the dishes, washing vegetables, chopping, cooking, cleaning. Rinse and repeat. The skin on my hands is eroding; bits get washed away under the tap and fall into the drain, reaching god knows where. Between chores, I remember to pop my pills. I try to be regular and sometimes even set alarms on my phone. But when the alarms go off, I forget why I set them. My husband has taught me to write the purpose against the alarm, but it’s too much of a bother. item.title: Raj Thackeray alleges Rs 18 crore stolen from Mumbai’s Siddhivinayak temple every year

Maharashtra Navnirman Sena chief Raj Thackeray on Sunday alleged that donations worth Rs 18 crore had been embezzled from the Siddhivinayak temple in Mumbai every year.

He also claimed that Rs 1,400 crore had been “stolen” from the Ram temple in Ayodhya.

The remarks came amid a row over the alleged embezzlement of donations at the Ram temple in Uttar Pradesh.

On Sunday, citing a letter purportedly written by eight temple trustees to Maharashtra Deputy Chief Minister Eknath Shinde, Thackeray claimed that employees at Siddhivinayak temple had siphoned off donations from collection boxes.

He also claimed that the temple’s weekly donations were below Rs 50 lakh before the alleged theft came to light, but increased to about Rs 1.5 crore after those allegedly involved were caught.

Sada Sarvankar, chairperson of the Siddhivinayak Temple Trust and a leader of the Eknath Shinde-led Shiv Sena, said that nine temple employees had been arrested in connection with the alleged theft, PTI reported.

“We have filed cases wherever required,” the news agency quoted Sarvankar as saying.

item.title: Kerala: 15 killed in rain-related incidents, seven missing

item.content:encoded:
The toll in rain-related incidents in Kerala has risen to 15, PTI quoted Chief Minister VD Satheesan as saying on Monday.

While he did not specify the period in which the deaths took place, the state has been receiving heavy and incessant rainfall since Friday, triggering flash floods and landslides.

Satheesan said on Monday that seven persons were missing amid the rains. Of these, two persons each were missing from Kollam and Kannur, and one each in Malappuram, Idukki and Muvattupuzha.

Malappuram had reported four deaths, while three persons died in Kottayam district. Two deaths each were reported in Ernakulam and Kollam, and one person each died in Idukki, Muvattupuzha and Kannur.

The chief minister announced that the state government will provide Rs 10,000 in funeral expenses to the families of those who died. Persons returning home from relief camps would receive Rs 10,000 as an immediate measure.

Additionally, an ex gratia of Rs 8 lakh was announced for the families of those who died. A compensation of Rs 12 lakh will be given to those who lost their homes and land due to landslides. Rs 6 lakh will be provided for families to rebuild their homes, said Satheesan.

The monk, who was formerly associated with the International Society for Krishna Consciousness, has been in jail since November 25, 2024. He was arrested for allegedly disrespecting Bangladesh’s national flag during a rally on October 25 that year in Chittagong.

He is the spokesperson of the Sammilito Sanatani Jagaron Jote, an organisation that advocates for the rights of Hindus and other minorities in Bangladesh.

The two cases in which he was granted bail on Sunday pertain to attempted murder and obstructing police officers from discharging their duties.

The Act allows for long periods of detention without trial up to a year.

The police had alleged that he “unlawfully trespassed into the site of the Tea Tribes Museum and thereafter trespassed into the nearby ATDC [Assam Tourism Development Corporation] Hyatt project at Ingle Pathar with deadly weapons” during the protest.

On July 29, a sessions court in Golaghat granted bail to Doley, stating that the investigating officer had already recorded the statements of key witnesses and that there was no possibility of the accused concealing or tampering with evidence.

Ceuta, an autonomous city, sits on Morocco’s northern coast. The Spanish government has said almost all of the migrants have since returned to Morocco, and at least 57 have died.

Faced with doubts as to how and why this was able to happen, the public was left with only footage and photographs: people swimming and climbing onto Ceuta’s Tarajal beach, tens of thousands in a single day and night, scores dead.

item.title: How Shakespeare’s ‘The Tempest’ can help readers understand the hidden costs of AI
item.description: The play offers a useful means of understanding how power operates through hidden infrastructures.
item.content:encoded:
In the 400 years since his death, William Shakespeare’s work has been used as a lens through which to interpret countless developments he could never have anticipated – from modern psychology and political theory to colonialism and climate change. His writing possesses an uncanny ability to illuminate nearly every facet of the human condition.

Yet, as a decolonial scholar and an AI researcher, we believe that Shakespeare’s plays are now beginning to illuminate something beyond that as well – the emergent forms of artificial intelligence that increasingly shape and challenge our understanding of what it means to think, act and be.

AI tools have rapidly become part of many people’s everyday lives. Yet relatively few probably consider the physical infrastructure that makes these systems possible. Each prompt we send is processed in distant data centres: vast facilities that generate responses by predicting the most likely sequence of words based on patterns learned from enormous datasets.

This dynamic of distant, unseen control recalls Shakespeare’s The Tempest, a play that offers a useful means of understanding how power operates through hidden infrastructures.

In South Mumbai’s Mandvi Koliwada sits a terracotta-colored building bearing the name Janabai and Madhavrao Rokade Municipal School.

As is the case with public buildings in many Indian cities, the names of the personalities that adorn them are often unfamiliar. Some of them are linked to relatively recent politicians and cultural figures. A few of them have a deeper historical connection. The Rokade municipal school falls in the second category.

The school was established in 1879, making it one of Mumbai’s earliest modern schools. It was started by Madhavrao Rokade.

For anyone interested in Mumbai’s socio-political history from this period, Madhavrao Rokade is remembered as a key member and writer associated with the Satyashodhak movement. This was a movement started by Jotirao and Savitribai Phule in Pune in 1873 to confront the upper-caste dominance in everyday life and to work toward inculcating a sense of collective consciousness among Bahujan communities, especially through education.

Rokade contributed to this movement by starting and running this school for many years with limited support. He was also known for his periodic writings in the late 19th century in newspapers such as Dinbandhu (Brother of the Oppressed) and Shetkaryacha Kaivari (Protector of Farmers).

item.description: The government’s concessions have not disrupted the arrangement that produced these grievances in the first place.

In a little over a month, the Cockroach Janata Party-led student movement that began as a joke held one of the world’s most immovable governments to a single demand and won. When Dharmendra Pradhan resigned as education minister on July 25, the students who had occupied Jantar Mantar wept and embraced. Abhijeet Dipke, who founded the movement, fell to his knees.

Since coming to power in 2014, the Bharatiya Janata Party government has rarely bowed to public pressure, and almost never to the young. The repeal of the farm laws in 2021 is remembered because such retreats are so uncommon.

But a victory of this kind is most vulnerable in the days just after it is won, when the crowds go home and the terms of the settlement are set by the side that conceded – in this case, the government.

That a leaderless, meme-driven mobilisation extracted a cabinet resignation, compensation for the families of students who died by suicide after the leak of the NEET question, and a promise to drop police cases against protesters is a genuine achievement.

item.title: How lab-grown diamonds have changed the game
item.description: The saying goes that ‘diamonds are forever’. But what if the market for them isn’t?
item.content:encoded:
You’ve probably heard the saying “a diamond is forever”. What if the market for them – with its hefty price tags – isn’t?

Back in March, Rio Tinto ended production at its Diavik diamond mine in Canada after 23 years. Earlier this month, diamond mining company De Beers announced a two-year production pause at the company’s flagship Venetia mine in South Africa.

De Beers is majority-owned by global mining giant Anglo American. According to a Bloomberg report this week, Anglo is now in talks to sell its 85% stake for about US$1 billion – a tiny fraction of the US$18 billion it was valued at when taken private in 2001.

So, what’s going on? The industry certainly hasn’t run out of diamonds to mine. But current prices and costs have made continued production of natural diamonds harder to justify.

Over the past couple of decades, lab-grown diamonds have changed the game. Consumers are also reconsidering what makes a diamond valuable – and what responsible consumption means.

A lesson from aluminium

In the mid-nineteenth century, aluminium was treated as a luxury material and its value exceeded that of gold. While it was abundant in the Earth’s crust, it was difficult and expensive to isolate and refine.

item.title: Who was Homer, author of the ‘Odyssey’?
item.description: When the ‘Odyssey’ first began to circulate in ancient Greece, no one knew its author. The song seems to have created the singer, not the other way around.
item.content:encoded:
Who wrote the Odyssey?

Homer, obviously: that is what we’ve been told since the late 6th century BCE, when ancient Greeks started crediting the Odyssey to a blind bard from the rocky isle of Chios.

But this “Homer” appeared at least a century later than the poem itself. When the Odyssey first began to circulate in ancient Greece, no one knew its author. The song seems to have created the singer, not the other way around.

How can you have a poem without a poet? Two American researchers, Milman Parry and Albert Lord, came across a possible answer.

In the 1930s, Parry and Lord travelled to the Balkans to study still-living traditions of epic poetry. In Yugoslavia and Albania, they found bards who sang of heroes from long ago. These singers did not recite from a book. Most of them couldn’t read or write at all. Instead, they improvised their epics as they sang. They knew the story by heart, but told it in different words with each performance.

Balkan bards achieved this by relying on a stock of formulaic scenes, lines and phrases, which they combined on the spot. The formulae were passed down from teacher to student, so that all singers tended to sound alike.

This telltale style is just what we find in Homeric poetry....

item.title: Can fuel-reliant South Asia survive the next global conflict?
item.description: The oil-importing countries of Bangladesh, Pakistan and Sri Lanka must invest in building energy security.
item.content:encoded:
Amid signs that the US and Iran have paused their latest round of hostilities, it is time to examine the economies that the conflict effectively brought to a standstill this year.

In March 2026, when the exchange of threats and missiles choked the Strait of Hormuz, the bill landed on the doors of Dhaka, Islamabad and Colombo long before it reached Washington or Brussels.

The moment revealed itself less as a geopolitical crisis and more as unending queues for fuel in South Asia, with restaurants shuttered and households plunged into darkness by relentless load shedding.

Bangladesh, Pakistan and Sri Lanka – three countries with virtually no domestic oil reserves and no meaningful influence over global commodity prices – absorbed energy shocks for a war they did not cause. That is the nature of fossil-fuel dependence in South Asia, and it is not new. The 2008 oil price bubble and subsequent spike. The 2022 Russia‑Ukraine war in which Russia limited supplies and caused gas price shocks. These are other chapters in the same structural story.

What makes 2026 different is that alternatives now exist, they are affordable, and some of these countries have already begun deploying them. The question is whether they build on that foundation proactively before the next disruption, or patch the damage reactively...

President Droupadi Murmu on Friday gave her assent to the 2026 Public Examinations Prevention of Unfair Means Amendment Act, a day after Parliament passed the legislation.

The amendments were introduced on Monday following nationwide youth protests over alleged irregularities in competitive examinations.

The Act raises the punishment for using unfair means in public examinations from the current three to five years’ imprisonment to five to 10 years. It also increases the maximum fine from Rs 10 lakh to Rs 50 lakh.

One of the key provisions of the Act empowers the Union government to set up a Special Task Force to investigate paper leak offences. The probe by police, central investigating agencies or the task force would have to be completed within two months, it says.

The Act also requires state governments and Union Territory administrations to set up special fast track courts. Pending cases under the Act would also be transferred to these fast track courts and disposed of within three months of transfer.

If instances of paper leaks or other offences listed under the Act are found to be organised, the legislation proposes a minimum sentence of seven years and a fine of up to Rs 10 crore.

item.title: ‘The Business of Business Is Not Just Business’: A changing view of Indian corporate responsibility
item.description: The anthology brings together a diverse and accomplished set of minds to study how business can shape culture.
item.content:encoded:
The title of Sutapa Banerjee’s edited volume, The Business of Business Is (Not) Just Business, underlines something that few would argue against. The era when businesses could legitimately argue that the only responsibility they have is to their shareholders is behind us. The role of business is widely acknowledged to encompass a much larger range of stakeholders. Businesses are not exempt from society; they play an active role in shaping it not just in economic terms but also culturally. Employment, migration, gender, environment, aspirations, access to opportunity, public discourse and the very idea of progress are all shaped in some way or the other by business.

And the book’s declared intention is to examine this from the lens of behaviour on the ground. What actually shapes behaviour, what exactly is meant by change, what mechanisms help produce this change at ground level?

Building businesses

It brings together a diverse and accomplished set of minds to study these questions. The contributors include business leaders, investors, policymakers and domain specialists across questions of sustainability, inclusion, employment, gender, technology and corporate governance. Its range is considerable. Poonawalla was scheduled to begin a hunger strike at the Gandhi Smriti in the national capital at 10 am, to protest against the government’s Ethanol Blended Petrol programme.

The Union government has mandated that all petrol sold in the country be blended with 20% ethanol – a substance produced from sugarcane and food grain. The policy is aimed at reducing India’s dependency on fossil fuels, cutting greenhouse gas emissions and boosting income for sugarcane farmers.

However, consumers have complained that the new fuel mix damages engines and reduces their mileage.

Speaking with reporters on Saturday, Poonawalla claimed that the police informed him that he had been put under house arrest because “thousands of protesters” were expected to participate in the protest.

The police did not give him any documents explaining the action, Poonawalla alleged.

item.title: August Indian nonfiction: Six new titles that take a closer look at 79 years of independence
item.description: A journalist’s report from India’s Maoist hotbed, a genius mathematician’s biography, an examination of India’s social policy, and more.
item.content:encoded:
All information sourced from publishers.

DD Kosambi: One Life Many Worlds, Ram Ramaswamy

Historian. Mathematician. Marxist. Polymath. DD Kosambi defied labels. The range and intellectual heft of his scholarship was truly astounding, with fundamental contributions in differential geometry and analyses in mathematics, the Kosambi distance in genetics, a statistical analysis of ancient coin hoards, a radical reinterpretation of Indian history and stellar compilations of the poetry of Vidyakara and Bhartrhari-all this in addition to a firm commitment to world peace and environmental activism.

Yet, for a man who contributed so much to the Indian intellectual tradition, he remains largely unknown. Sixty years after his passing, there is scant recognition of his talents-he is quoted more often than he is read and praised more often than he is analysed.

Ram Ramaswamy’s biography of Kosambi seeks to correct this lapse. Set against the backdrop of fascinating social, political, scientific and historiographical transformation in the subcontinent, and drawing from letters, journal entries, family accounts and unprecedented archival material, DD Kosambi: One Life, Many Worlds reveals a rare incandescent genius and a fearless independent spirit with boundless curiosity-whose relevance in the fields of pedagogy, research and invention can be seen even today.

item.title: The story of Kerala’s first female writer-composer who transcended her time
item.description: Kuttykunju Thangkachi broke new ground in music, theatre and literature at a time when women’s creativity was expected to remain private.
item.content:encoded:
A gaunt elderly woman, her face sombre and framed by wispy grey hair left loose over her shoulders, gazes out in the side-profile. She wears the unmistakable symbols of an upper caste elite woman from 19th-century Kerala: the mundu mulakacha wrap tied across her chest, layers of gold around her neck, and a yawning ear piercing that signals a lifetime of wearing heavy gold earrings. Yet to dismiss Kuttykunju Thangkachi as merely a privileged noblewoman would be a profound mistake.

The tumultuous 84 years of her life, which ended in 1904, were packed with triumphs virtually unheard of for women of her era. She was the earliest female dramatist in Malayalam with her play Ajnatavasam, the first woman to write attakathas, or librettos, for Kathakali, and a prolific creator across Kerala’s indigenous musical forms, including kummi, thiruvathira pattu, kurathipattu and thullal. Crucially, she was the first female Carnatic composer from Kerala at a time when only men were accorded the elevated title of vaggeyakara (writer-composer).

The suspected militants had opened fire at them in the Kellam area of Kulgam. Following the attack, the security forces cordoned off the area and began a search operation to track down the assailants.

item.content:encoded:
Booker Prize-shortlisted author Avni Doshi’s new novel, The First House, is here. And it is magnificent. A terrifying story of heartbreak, humiliation, and total annihilation of the self, the novel burns through the skin, scorching the very heart.

The novel starts with the narrator’s husband asking for a divorce. She had believed them to be reasonably happy, but after two daughters, the husband would beg to differ. The reasons are the usual – he feels trapped, he’s bored, the wife is too much. She proceeds to remind him of his responsibilities, especially towards his children. It’s a deadlock. item.title: ‘The Good Reporter’: The women journalists of Khabar Lahariya tell their stories on their own terms
item.description: The ‘journalism memoir’ is written by ten women from the Khabar Lahariya collective, alongside journalist and co-founder Disha Mullick.
item.content:encoded:
At some point in the early years of Khabar Lahariya, a story about a stolen buffalo calf made the front page. The women who put it there understood that the theft of a calf in rural UP was not a minor story dressed up as news. It was a story about inter-caste harassment, about whose losses count and who gets to decide what the public needs to investigate. The Good Reporter: A Memoir of Journalism in the 21st Century is a memoir about journalism built on that understanding.

The book opens with a warning. “This is a somewhat elliptical, unreliable autobiography of ten very different women,” it says before you have properly settled in. The story of what this collective has done over two decades of rural journalism in UP “has always been a better story to tell than how we have done it and keep doing it.” That distinction between the what versus the how is what the entire book turns on. If you came for the rousing version, the collective has already clocked you.

January 13,1984: I was 16, and it was the first football match I had watched with my own eyes rather than through the grain of a Doordarshan transmission. My father and I were among the 80,000 football fans crowded into Eden Gardens, for a Nehru Cup encounter between an unfancied India and mighty Argentina.

A video clip of that game resurfaced on YouTube a couple of weeks ago and refreshed three of my lasting memories of the game. The first is of disappointment: Diego Maradona, already reckoned to be the best player of his generation, had stayed home. But the Argentines were not lacking in quality. item.title: In Nicaragua, President Ortega bans elections – a new page in the authoritarian playbook
item.description: This shows a growing brazenness among autocratic regimes and a declining concern for international legitimacy.
item.content:encoded:
Since being elected for a second term as Nicaraguan president in 2006, Daniel Ortega – the former Sandinista freedom fighter-turned-authoritarian leader – has extended his term of office several times. But last week he announced a new strategy for holding on to power.

He declared that there will no longer be elections in the Central American country. Making a speech to commemorate the anniversary of the 1979 revolution that toppled the Somoza dictatorship which had ruled Nicaragua since 1937, he said: “The days when parties backed by the Yankees and the Somocistas would return to power are over – never again.” The legal changes are already moving through the country’s legislature.

Nicaragua’s elections have long been rigged and repressive. But this marks a new scale of authoritarian rule. The elimination of elections is a rare and extreme case, even in today’s landscape of authoritarian regimes. So this reflects a worrying trend of brazenness on the part of Nicaragua’s president.

Spin dictators

Most modern autocrats are what researchers call “spin dictators”. They invest in a democratic disguise and the careful curation of a public image fostered by propaganda and misinformation. Elections play a central role in this playbook.

Congress MP KC Venugopal on Friday moved a privilege motion against Union Minister of State Jitendra Singh, objecting to his claim that “no firing” took place during student protests outside Parliament on July 20.

Singh made the statement in the Lok Sabha on Wednesday during a debate on the anti-paper leak bill

According to the notice sent by Venugopal to Speaker Om Birla, the minister said that “no firing took place at all” and that only tear gas had been used.

However, Venugopal said in his notice that “contrary to the minister’s assertions, firing did occur”, and alleged that Singh had “knowingly and deliberately provided incorrect information to Parliament and misled the House”.

item.title: Deluge with monsoon deficit is India’s new climate normal
item.description: Climate change is no longer about more or less rainfall but is redistributing water in increasingly unpredictable ways.
item.content:encoded:
In the first week of July, in Mumbai’s Mankhurd, torrential monsoon rains triggered a building collapse that buried five children beneath the debris, transforming one of the city’s wettest July days in half a century into a humanitarian tragedy. Streets disappeared beneath floodwaters, transport networks ground to a halt, and emergency services struggled to reach stranded residents.

Thousands of kilometres away, London faced an entirely different manifestation of the same crisis. During the June 2026 heatwave, temperatures exceeded 36 degrees celsius, commuters fainted inside sweltering Underground trains, and climate activists covered Tube stations with stickers reading, “Heatwave, sponsored by Shell”, highlighting the perceived role of fossil fuels in intensifying global warming.

These events unfolded in vastly different economic and geographic settings. Yet they reflected a common reality: climate change no longer distinguishes between developed and developing nations. Whether through floods, heatwaves, landslides or dust storms, extreme weather is increasingly becoming the defining challenge of the twenty-first century.

The scientific evidence underpinning this reality has become overwhelming. The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) reported in 2023 that the global mean near-surface temperature in 2023 was 1.45 ± 0.12 degrees celsius above the pre-industrial average, bringing the world dangerously close to the 1.5 degrees celsius threshold established under the Paris Agreement.

item.title: Delhi violence: Ex-AAP councillor Tahir Hussain, four others get life term for IB staffer’s murder
item.description: The judge rejected the Delhi Police’s plea for the death penalty and said that capital punishment is the ‘last resort’.
item.content:encoded:
A Delhi court on Friday sentenced former Aam Aadmi Party councilor Tahir Hussain and four others to life imprisonment for the murder of Intelligence Bureau staffer Ankit Sharma during the 2020 riots in the national capital, Bar and Bench reported.

Additional Sessions Judge Praveen Singh of the Karkardooma Court rejected the Delhi Police’s plea for the death penalty and said capital punishment is the “last resort”, The Indian Express reported.

The court held that the convicts were not beyond reformation and could be “disciplined and made to follow rules”.

However, the judge described the crime as being committed with “utmost brutality” and called the barbarity involved “nauseating and sickening”, the newspaper reported.

The court noted that the prosecution had not presented evidence showing that the convicts had a violent disposition or a tendency to commit such offences.

It also said there was no evidence of previous violent crimes and that their conduct in custody had been “entirely satisfactory”, apart from minor infractions, Bar and Bench reported.

The Delhi Police had sought the death penalty, arguing that Sharma’s murder was brutal and cold-blooded.

“Those who want mercy should also show mercy,” the police’s counsel had said.

The defence opposed the plea, arguing that the death penalty should only be awarded in the rarest of rare cases.

The Supreme Court on Friday stayed the arrest of Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam MLA V Senthil Balaji in a corruption case linked to the Tamil Nadu State Marketing Corporation, or Tasmac, subject to his cooperation with the investigation, Live Law reported.

Tasmac is a government-owned company that has a monopoly over the wholesale and retail sales of alcoholic beverages in the state.

A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi passed the interim order while hearing the MLA’s appeal against the Madras High Court’s decision on Thursday to deny him anticipatory bail.

However, the bench directed him to surrender his passport and barred him from influencing witnesses or tampering with evidence, the legal news outlet reported.

The chief justice questioned the state’s counsel on why custodial interrogation was necessary when the case was largely based on documentary evidence.

item.description: The festival was held earlier to showcase some of the most historic spots and events of the Indian independence movement.

Ferozepur, a garrison border town in Punjab abutting the present-day India-Pakistan border, hosted the first edition of the Ferozepur Heritage, Military, and Literary Festival earlier this year – the result of a collaboration between The Military Literature Festival Association, Chandigarh, the Golden Arrow Division and the Ferozepur Literati Association. The Festival aimed to raise awareness about the rich heritage of the region, promote tourism, and showcase the glorious legacy of the Indian Armed Forces. The festival successfully transformed its primary venues – Dass and Brown World School and Sunder Singh Stadium, Ferozepur Cantt – into hubs of intellectual discourse and military pride, bringing together gallantry award winners, literary scholars, and thousands of residents.

item.content:encoded:
Exiled Bangladesh-born author Taslima Nasreen returned to Kolkata on Friday for the first time in nearly 19 years ahead of a literary event, PTI reported.

Nasreen arrived at Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose International Airport and told reporters: “I'm feeling very good to be back”.

The visit marks her first return to Kolkata since November 2007, when she was forced to leave the city after some Muslim fundamentalists claimed that her autobiographical book Dwikhandito had hurt their religious sentiments.

As protests escalated and the Army was deployed to restore order in parts of Kolkata, the then Left Front government led by Buddhadeb Bhattacharjee asked Nasreen to leave the city.

Nasreen has lived in exile since fleeing Bangladesh in 1994 after receiving death threats over her for her writings, particularly Lajja, her novel examining the persecution of Bangladesh’s Hindu minority in the aftermath of the Babri Masjid demolition in Ayodhya.

She had initially settled in Kolkata in 2004, where she spent three years and described the city as her second home before being asked to leave during the unrest in 2007.

Tirkey also said that Hockey India’s Executive Board was not consulted before the change was implemented, The Indian Express reported.

The federation said the blue jersey blended with the blue synthetic playing surface used in international hockey, affecting visibility, and that players and coaches had suggested alternative colours, including saffron and yellow.

The jersey also has darker patterns to “celebrate India’s rich cultural heritage”. The federation said that the change “embodies the spirit of Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat [One India, Supreme India]”.

item.title: Arundhati Roy: ‘I’ve been angry for a long time, but I laugh with anger, as did those students’
item.description: Scroll’s Supriya Sharma takes a walk at Jantar Mantar with the writer-activist.
item.content:encoded:
On Monday morning, a day after education minister Dharmendra Pradhan quit the Modi government, writer and activist Arundhati Roy gamely agreed to come with us to Jantar Mantar.

For 36 days, hundreds of young people had camped there to demand Pradhan’s resignation. The protest had escalated last week after a police crackdown brought thousands into the streets, many of whom openly mocked and ridiculed Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Apart from the one time she publicly showed up to support the protestors, Roy told us she made several trips to Jantar Mantar in disguise. The jokes, memes, slogans targeting Modi, she said, left her cheeks “aching from smiling so much”.

Khalid has sought an interim bail on the same ground on which two other suspects – Tasleem Ahmad and Abdul Khalid Saifi – were granted six months’ interim bail by the Supreme Court on May 22, the newspaper reported.

How have India’s youth used satire and sarcasm to create a new grammar of protest? What has caused the crisis of education in India? Can it be resolved merely with the resignation of the education minister?

In this episode of Yeh Daagh Daagh Ujala, writer and activist Harsh Mander talks with Zoya Hasan, Saroj Giri, and Yamini Aiyar about the student protests that have spread across the country this year – and why they’re about so much more than the one incident that set them off.

Political scientist Zoya Hasan is Professor Emerita, Jawaharlal Nehru University, and Distinguished Professor, Council for Social Development. Saroj Giri is an associate professor in the department of political science at Delhi University. Yamini Aiyer is the former president and chief executive of the Centre for Policy Research.

Their conversation digs into jobless growth, exam scams and a public education system that’s been failing young people for years. item.description: The court has ordered the release of Vinay Kulkarni and eight others on bail while their appeals are pending.
item.content:encoded:
The Karnataka High Court on Friday suspended the life sentences of former Congress MLA Vinay Kulkarni and eight others convicted for the murder of Bharatiya Janata Party member Yogesh Gowda in 2016, Bar and Bench reported.

A bench of Justices Mohammad Nawaz and G Basavaraja ordered their release on bail while their appeals are pending.

The suspension of the sentence paves the way for Kulkarni to be restored as an MLA. He was disqualified as a legislator in May based on his conviction, The Hindu reported.

The court on Friday also suspended the seven-year sentence imposed on suspended police officer Channakeshava B Tingarikar and ordered his release on bail, the legal news outlet reported.

On April 15, a special court in Bengaluru had convicted Kulkarni along with 15 others in the murder case. Two days later, it sentenced the Congress leader to life imprisonment.

Gowda was killed in June 2016. The case had been investigated by the Central Bureau of Investigation.

The central agency had filed a chargesheet for murder, criminal conspiracy, public servant disobeying the law to shield a person accused in a matter, destruction of evidence, rioting and illegal possession of weapons.
